title: Serving runtime: architecture, kernel scheduling, profiling & runbooks
author: Michael Chen
content:
Overview:
This document consolidates the serving runtime architecture, kernel scheduling design, profiling and benchmarking playbooks, known issues and operational runbooks used by the Serving Runtime team. It is intended to be the one-stop reference for engineers onboarding to the runtime team and for on-call responders handling production incidents.

Audience and scope:
- Audience: runtime engineers, infra, SRE, performance engineers, and solutions/SEs working on Dedicated/Private deployments.
- Scope: architecture diagrams, kernel scheduler logic, profiling procedures, benchmark suite usage, release checklist, known issues, and primary runbooks for incidents and capacity operations.

High-level architecture (summary):
- FrontDoor service: TLS termination, auth, rate limiting, API validation (owner: eng-platform).
- Router (request router): policy-based routing (latency/cost/region), model variant selection, and KV cache lookup (owner: runtime-routing).
- Scheduler (kernel scheduler & executor): packs requests into micro-batches, places work on GPU worker pools, performs kernel selection and quantization path selection (owner: runtime-scheduler).
- ModelWorkers (worker pool): model weight loader, KV cache management, per-GPU inference engine, kernel runtime (owner: runtime-exec).
- StateStore/Cache: prefix/KV cache, persistent caching layer (Redis + local on-GPU KV cache) (owner: platform-storage).
- Telemetry/Tracing: structured logs, per-token metrics, and sampling (owner: observability).

Design goals and SLOs:
- Tail latency SLO: 99th percentile generation latency < 150ms for text-gen (seq <= 128) on standard latency pool; 99.9th < 500ms.
- Availability SLO: 99.95% per region for Hosted API endpoints.
- Throughput goal: sustain target tokens/sec per GPU as defined in model profiles (see benchmarking suite).
- Cost-efficiency: intelligent batching and cache hit-rate > 60% for interactive workloads.

Kernel scheduling and execution model:
- Scheduling primitives:
  - Micro-batching window: adjustable (default 4ms) that groups compatible requests by model, precision (fp16/int8), and sequence length bucket.
  - Affinity groups: pin long-lived KV-cached sessions to preferred worker to maximize KV cache locality.
  - Preemption: short jobs can preempt lower-priority background batches when latency SLOs are at risk.
- Kernel selection heuristics:
  1. Inspect model profile (architecture, seq distribution, quantization support).
  2. If sequence <= 128 and model supports fused-attn kernel, choose fused kernel path.
  3. If quantized weights available and workload is cost-sensitive, select int8 path with fallback to fp16 on quality/regression detection.
  4. Consider device memory pressure and KV cache locality when selecting placement.
- Key scheduling thresholds (default):
  - micro_batch_ms: 4ms
  - max_micro_batch_size: 32 requests
  - preempt_latency_threshold_99: 140ms
  - kv_affinity_ttl: 10m

Profiling and benchmarking playbook (step-by-step):
1) Local profiling (developer machine):
   - Build a representative payload set (see prompt-sets-and-benchmarks).
   - Use the local profiler: ./tools/runtime_profiler --model <model> --seq 128 --threads 4 --out profile.json
   - Inspect flame graphs: ./tools/pprof --input profile.json --html > profile.html
2) Fleet-level profiling:
   - Schedule profiling job via k8s job that runs synthetic traffic at target p95/p99 load.
   - Collect per-GPU metrics: GPU utilization, SM occupancy, memory copy times, kernel latencies.
   - For distributed tracing, enable sample rate 1% to prevent telemetry overload.
3) Kernel-level investigations:
   - Reproduce highest-latency kernel using the kernel-replay tool: ./kernel_replay --trace <trace-id> --kernel-id <id>
   - Compare alternative kernels by setting environment variable KERNEL_OVERRIDE in the worker and re-running benchmark.

Benchmark suite (usage and outputs):
- Location: repo: infra/serving-benchmarks (see related pages).
- Bench modes: latency, throughput, mixed.
- Example run (throughput):
  ./bench/run_bench.sh --model redwood-7b --mode throughput --tokens 1_000_000 --batch_size 16 --quant int8
- Output artifacts: csv summary, per-kernel histogram, SLO compliance report (HTML).
- Benchmark matrix: each model has an entry in quantization-profiles with expected tokens/sec per GPU for each precision and sequence length. Use these to validate fleet capacity planning.

Release notes checklist (runtime component):
1. Update model profiles and quantization metadata.
2. Run benchmark suite across staging cluster and compare to previous baseline.
3. Smoke tests: cold-start, KV cache warm, prefix-caching TTL scenarios.
4. Canary rollout: 5% traffic -> 25% -> 100% with automated rollback on latency regression > 10% p99.
5. Observability: ensure new metrics are instrumented and dashboards updated.
6. Post-release validation: run golden prompt set to detect quality regressions.

Known issues (operational):
- Issue #KRN-201: occasional p99 latency spikes when KV cache eviction coincides with high micro-batching. Mitigation: increase kv_affinity_ttl to 15m and stagger eviction windows (workaround applied).
- Issue #KRN-217: int8 path has occasional hallucination regression for specific prompts on redwood-13b-v1. Workaround: fall back to fp16 when similarity-based quality check fails.
- Issue #KRN-230: node-level OOMs during model load on mixed-workload GPU pools. Mitigation: ensure model prefetch pipeline pre-allocates memory and use model memory cap.

Operational runbooks (quick reference):
A) High p99 latency incident (page on-call immediately):
  1. Pager triggers; on-call triage (runtime lead): check FrontDoor error rate and Router drop rate.
  2. Run: kubectl -n runtime get pods -l app=model-worker -o wide and inspect pod restarts and GPU memory.
  3. Check metrics: dashboards/serving/runtime/p99-latency and logs for kernel errors.
  4. If KV-cache miss rate > 30% and latency spike correlated, temporarily increase kv_affinity_ttl and scale worker pool.
  5. If kernel OOM or CUDA errors present, mark affected nodes cordoned and trigger auto-remediation: ./tools/drain_gpu_node --node <node-name> --reason "kernel-oom"
  6. If canary rollback needed, run rollout rollback: ./infra/rollout --service runtime-scheduler --to previous
  7. Post-incident: run profiling job, open a ticket in JIRA, and schedule RCA.

B) Degraded throughput (sustained lower tokens/sec):
  1. Validate benchmark artifacts and compare with stored baseline in infra/benchmarks/artifacts/<date>.csv.
  2. Inspect batching windows and micro-batch hit rate: query metrics micro_batch_fill_rate.
  3. If batching reduced, lower micro_batch_ms to 3ms for latency-insensitive workloads or increase max_micro_batch_size.
  4. Scale worker pools and ensure autoscaler is healthy.

C) Release rollback procedure (emergency):
  1. Initiate incident channel and notify product/security if customer-facing.
  2. Stop traffic to release: ./infra/traffic_ctl --service runtime --set-traffic old-version=100
  3. Roll back scheduler config and restart affected pods: kubectl rollout undo deployment/runtime-scheduler --namespace runtime
  4. Validate with golden prompt set before re-opening traffic.

Team wiki and onboarding notes:
- Quickstart for new engineers: 1) clone infra/serving-runtime, 2) run local dev cluster with docker-compose dev.yaml, 3) run unit and integration tests: make test-unit && make test-integ, 4) follow profiling playbook to generate your first profile.

Appendices and artifacts:
- Example config snippet (k8s config):
  apiVersion: v1
  kind: ConfigMap
  metadata:
    name: runtime-scheduler-config
  data:
    micro_batch_ms: "4"
    max_micro_batch_size: "32"
    preempt_latency_threshold_99: "140"

- Useful CLI/debug commands:
  - ./tools/runtime_profiler --list-models
  - kubectl -n runtime logs <pod> --since=1h | grep "kernel-error"
  - ./tools/drain_gpu_node --node <node-name> --reason <reason>
